extracted.intended_audience: anatomists, physicians, natural philosophers, and experimental naturalists (readers of the Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and experimental investigation in anatomy and natural history: careful dissection, comparative observation across species/conditions, quantitative field measurements, and descriptions of apparatus and procedures for reproducible demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissect and record parts in their natural state
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine and draw parts in that state in which they are found naturally, without at all forcing them; thereby to find whether the parts are indeed joined together or separated, and what situation is assigned them by nature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manipulating tissues so as to create artifactual relations; base anatomical drawings and descriptions on the part's unforced, observed configuration. Example anti-pattern: forcing parts into positions that misrepresent natural attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for earlier operations and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect upon all the operations made before coming to a part, which may have caused some change in its situation, connexion, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting dissection results, document prior incisions, removals, or treatments that could have altered morphology or relationships; use this to interpret current observations and to defend against objections that changes are artefactual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary dissection methods; do not adhere to fixed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the ways of dissecting; avoid binding ourselves to certain fixed laws of dissecting each part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ multiple dissection approaches to reveal different aspects of structure; consider alternate preparations rather than a single traditional technique. Rationale: different techniques may reveal otherwise hidden features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assert function without structural knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to explain the motions (or uses) of parts if the fabric of the parts be not known; anatomists are ridiculous who discourse magisterially of the use of parts which they know not the structure of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit functional claims to those supported by demonstrated structure; avoid speculative statements about use when anatomical architecture is not established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative sampling across species, developmental stages, and pathological states
rubrics_metrics.description: For acquiring good knowledge of the brain (and other parts) there must be dissections and examinations of as many heads as there are different species of animals, and different states and conditions of each kind; fetuses and brains changed by sickness often reveal features not seen in sound entire brains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare specimens from multiple species, ages (including fetuses), and diseased conditions to infer development, variation, and hidden structures. Example: fetuses may show formation processes invisible in adult organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple preparation techniques to reveal tissue composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare specimens by boiling, broiling, infusion in spirit of wine (hot and cold), expansion on glass, etc., to inspect whether a tissue is composed of vessels and liquids or an intermediate substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a variety of physical and chemical preparations to test competing anatomical hypotheses (e.g., parenchyma vs. congeries of vessels). Report which techniques were used and what each revealed; note limitations (e.g., drying during expansion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate vessel continuity by injection and visual markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that tubes are real cavities by injecting coloured fluid into an artery (or arteria praesparans) so that injected matter discolours parts; opening the part then shows tubes containing the injected matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use injections (dyes, and ideally mercury where available) as experimental controls to show internal continuity of vessels rather than mere surface staining. Document the injection site, the agent used, and subsequent observations. Anticipate objections (e.g., exterior colouration) and design tests (see next criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct tests (pricking/opening) to show internal contents
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure coloured particles are included within cavities and not merely external, moisten and then prick/open a containing tube with a fine needle; observe whether liquid particles issue forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include definitive manipulations that distinguish between internal vs. external deposition of markers. Describe the manipulation and outcome to rebut alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document macroscopic demonstrations (expansion, extension) to show continuity and texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand and extend parts on glass so that vessels can be seen to continue from one end to the other, sometimes extending half a yard before breaking; such extension preserves figure and magnitude unless drying occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide figures/plates of expanded preparations and describe observed continuity, fragility, and changes on drying. Use these macroscopic demonstrations to support interpretations about tubular composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize cautiously across organs while noting exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesise broad principles (e.g., many so-called glands are congeries of vessels and their liquors) but acknowledge observed small membranes or remnants in some animals that may serve as intermediate substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing general anatomical claims, report the range of observations, exceptions, and opposing expert opinions; invite further autopsy-based confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field sampling and comparative description for geological/volcanic materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect samples from diverse distances and positions (top/mouth, 1 mile, 4 miles, 10 miles, skirts); note differences such as dryness vs. moisture, physical form (hard lumps vs. soft dirty grains), crusts (brimstone), taste (vitriolate), and spatial distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically sample and describe material variation with distance and location to infer eruption processes and transport. Report both qualitative properties and their spatial relationship to the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement of brine strength by controlled weighing and evaporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh a known quart volume bottle filled with distilled water (mark), then fill to same mark with brine, weigh, boil away the water to dryness without additions or clarification, and weigh the salt obtained to compute proportion; repeat at different times to detect temporal changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful mass measurements and controlled evaporation to derive salt concentration. Control for temporal extraction effects (brine can strengthen after working) and tidal myths by repeating measures at different dates and recording working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe environmental and production context for industrial-natural observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Record pit depth, topography (low grounds, mosses), vegetation, proximity to rivers, existence/absence of shells or specific earth types, temperature of spring water, and details of local manufacturing practice (pan sizes, fuel, scumming mixtures, sequence of boiling and refilling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both natural context and human production methods when studying resources (salt springs). This includes measurements, qualitative notes, and the exact working procedures used locally, since these influence observed properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical case reporting: provide full narrative, measurements, interventions, and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Present patient demographics, precise chronology of onset, physical findings (e.g., breast circumferences, estimated weights, hardness of tubuli), treatments proposed or applied (emollients, purgatives, diuretics, phlebotomy), rationale, subsequent observations (ulcers, discharge), follow-up interventions, and final outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply measurable data and sequential observations so readers can evaluate the diagnosis and therapeutic reasoning. Avoid speculative cures; explain why certain radical proposals (e.g., amputation) were rejected in favor of conservative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument description should include geometrical principle and a working model
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the geometric demonstration for the instrument's function (e.g., grinding hyperbolical surfaces by rotation/attrition of bodies with specified axes) and, if possible, a physical model of the machine; minute descriptions of every part may be omitted when geometrical principles suffice to reconstruct it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain axes, relative positions, motions, and roles of parts (director, grinding tool, lens). When space is limited, give geometric proof and a model so artisans can infer construction; nevertheless indicate essential components and their relations.
